sources.title: Human History Map, world-1650 historical-basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded with topojson-client. The exact malaya feature is a two-part MultiPolygon with 178 positions and bbox 100.1404,0.7264 to 119.0442,6.8996. It includes tested Malacca, Johor Bahru, Kuala Lumpur, Penang and Kota Kinabalu points, but excludes Kota Bharu, Kuala Terengganu, Singapore, Kuching and Bandar Seri Begawan.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1914 historical-basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded with topojson-client. The 1914-1920 target repeats the same two-part, 178-position footprint as every earlier malaya interval. Static geometry cannot encode the period’s changing sultanates, colonies, protectorates, settlements or company rule.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, Old Johor kingdom
sources.note: National Library reference article checked. Johor gained Dutch trade and military support after helping take Melaka in 1641; it remained powerful in the seventeenth century, faced a succession crisis after Mahmud II was killed in 1699, incorporated Bugis power, split between rival British- and Dutch-backed claimants after 1812, and was divided into spheres by the 1824 treaty.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, Mother Island: Finding Singapore's Past in Pulau Lingga
sources.note: Historian Faris Joraimi's article checked. It explains the Johor-Riau system of Malay sultans and Bugis viceroys, eighteenth-century Riau trade, the Dutch victory of 1784, the 1819 Singapore arrangement and 1824 partition. It also documents Orang Laut, Malay, Bugis and Teochew networks, fish traps, sago, houses, boats and pastimes while distinguishing present practice from direct period evidence.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, On Paper: Singapore Before 1867
sources.note: National Library exhibition article checked. It explains the rival British and Dutch claims surrounding Singapore, the 1824 treaty exchange, the split of the Johor-Riau Sultanate into European spheres and the treaty's long-lived border consequences.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Melaka and George Town
sources.note: UNESCO property description checked. Melaka and George Town preserve five centuries of trading and cultural exchange and successive Malay, Portuguese, Dutch and British influences, including government buildings, religious structures, shophouses, townhouses, food, languages and festivals.

sources.title: UK Parliament Hansard, Federation of Malaya Independence Bill, 12 July 1957
sources.note: Colonial Secretary's retrospective parliamentary account checked critically. It dates the Penang settlement to 1786, British acquisition of Melaka to 1824, treaties and advisers in Malay states from the 1870s, the four-state federation to 1896 and the nine Malay states as constitutionally distinct from the Straits Settlements. It also describes the 1957 independence legislation from the British government's viewpoint.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, Thomas Braddell
sources.note: National Library biography checked. It identifies Thomas Braddell as a colonial official involved in concluding the 1874 Pangkor Treaty. The page documents one British participant, not a neutral or complete account of Perak politics.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, From Sea to Road: Building the Causeway
sources.note: Archive-based article checked. It gives rubber and tin production near 1900, railway consolidation in 1906, the Gemas-Johor Bahru line in 1909, train-ferry traffic, construction beginning in 1919 and the Causeway foundation ceremony in April 1920. It distinguishes the project's later completion in 1924.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, Remembering Singapore's Railway Lines and Stations
sources.note: Architecture historian Lai Chee Kien's article checked. It dates the Taiping-Port Weld railway to 1885, Kuala Lumpur-Klang to 1886, continuous public transport from Penang to Singapore to 1909, and notes Tamil railway labor and associated Hindu shrines. It also explains that rail served colonial tin and rubber economies.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Anti-colonial raced capitalism in Malaysia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article checked at its colonial-economy discussion. It describes British protectorate treaties, Chinese and Indian migrant labor in mines and plantations, indenture until 1914, harsh conditions, Malay peasant food production and colonial devaluation of women's household work.

sources.title: Sabah Government, People and History
sources.note: Official state overview checked. It identifies numerous Indigenous communities and languages; describes Kadazan-Dusun farming and fishing, Murut longhouses and agriculture, Bajau farming, fishing, diving and horsemanship; and dates North Borneo Chartered Company rule from 1881. The community descriptions are broad present-day summaries with historical continuity, not a 1900 census.

sources.title: Sabah State Attorney-General's Chambers, British North Borneo Company Charter, 1881
sources.note: Official legal archive page checked for the royal charter granted to the British North Borneo Company on 1 November 1881. The charter is evidence of company authority claimed under British law, not proof that every Indigenous community consented or was effectively governed.

sources.title: Sabah Government Printing Department, history
sources.note: Official department history checked. The company government established its press at Kudat in 1883 and issued the North Borneo Herald and Official Gazette; the press moved to Sandakan in 1885 and Jesselton in 1918. This documents colonial administration and print, not general literacy.

sources.title: Kota Kinabalu City Hall, early city history
sources.note: Official municipal history checked. It records a pre-existing Bajau settlement at Gaya Bay, a company post founded in 1882, Mat Salleh's destruction of the Gaya settlement in 1897, and the subsequent move to mainland Api-Api/Jesselton as a port and railway stop.

sources.title: British Museum, woman's girdle from Sabah, As1912,18
sources.note: Museum catalogue checked. It dates a woman's rattan-and-brass girdle to the 1850s-1910 and records that a former Murut attribution was corrected to Dusun after consultation with Sabah Museum. The object is one collected garment component, not a universal costume.

sources.title: Museum Volunteers, National Museum of Malaysia, Malay architecture and traditional houses
sources.note: Museum-volunteer report of architect Ahmad Najib Ariffin's 2022 talk checked. It describes raised, ventilated, modular timber houses; a main family and guest room, sleeping area and kitchen annex; and bathrooms and latrines placed away from the main house. It is a modern architectural interpretation of a varied vernacular tradition, not a household census for 1650-1920.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, Travelling hawkers
sources.note: National Library reference article checked. It describes nineteenth- and early twentieth-century itinerant work, affordable meals, children selling snacks, vendors using baskets, yokes and carts, Malay, Javanese, Chinese and Indian foods, and licensing extended to day and itinerant hawkers in 1919. Most evidence is Singapore-specific and therefore regional context outside the polygon.

sources.title: National Heritage Board Singapore, Terengganu sarong
sources.note: Asian Civilisations Museum object record checked. The late nineteenth- to early twentieth-century Terengganu sarong is a tubular lower-body garment made with weft ikat and gold supplementary-weft songket, with a front panel described for women. It is one museum object, not everybody's clothing.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, Malay school-book printing and publishing
sources.note: National Library research article checked. It gives Straits Settlements Malay vernacular enrollment of 22 percent for boys and 2 percent for girls in 1901, the Government Malay Press from 1885, school use of Malay newspapers and book distribution beyond the settlements to Malay states, Johor and Borneo.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, Jawi Peranakkan, 1876-1895
sources.note: National Library collection article checked. Jawi Peranakkan was a Malay weekly in Jawi script printed in Singapore, with news, advertising, government notices, poetry and school readers; circulation was limited and aimed largely at literate Arab, Indian and Baba Peranakan elites. It also records debates over health, education and language.

sources.title: British Library, Johor letter to Napoleon III, Or 16126
sources.note: British Library catalogue checked. The illuminated Malay letter in Jawi was sent by Temenggung Ibrahim of Johor in 1857. The catalogue supplies a Latin-script transliteration beginning Bahawa ini surat and an English translation beginning This is a letter; digital images are currently unavailable, so the sample is not presented as a facsimile.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, Early nursing in Singapore
sources.note: Archive-based article checked. It documents limited colonial hospital access, home birth with Malay bidan, French nuns nursing from 1885, qualified nurses from 1900, Asian midwife training from 1910, household infant-health visits from 1911 and compulsory midwife registration in 1915. Evidence is mainly Singapore and must not be generalized across the peninsula or North Borneo.

sources.title: National Library Board Singapore, Cholera in nineteenth-century Singapore
sources.note: Archive-based article checked. It documents cholera, inadequate water and hospital capacity, lack of a sewage system in 1889, cesspits and bucket collection of night soil, and sanitation measures after the 1895 epidemic. These are Singapore-specific examples within the wider Straits world.

sources.title: Malaysia Institute for Medical Research, history
sources.note: Official institute history checked. A Pathological Institute was proposed in 1900 and opened in Kuala Lumpur in 1901 to research malaria, beri-beri and other diseases. Early work covered mosquitoes, malaria control, dysentery and later evidence that excessive rice milling contributed to beri-beri.

sources.title: NCBI Bookshelf, Mosquito utopias and dystopias
sources.note: Scholarly chapter checked. Malcolm Watson began malaria-control work in Klang in 1900; drainage and environmental changes reduced cases in specific towns and protected port development. Results belong to targeted colonial projects and did not mean malaria or unequal medical access disappeared.

sources.title: Government of Malaysia, Malaysian history
sources.note: Official national summary checked for later chronology. The Federation of Malaya became independent in 1957 and joined Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore to form Malaysia in 1963. These later events show why the atlas's 1920 change from malaya to malaysia is anachronistic.

sources.title: National Archives of Malaysia, “Pemasyhuran Malaysia”: Lahirnya Sebuah Negara
sources.note: National Archives account checked for the 1957 independence proclamation and the agreement and proclamation that formed Malaysia with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore on 16 September 1963. It is used only to distinguish those later milestones from the atlas's premature 1920 relabeling.

proposedOverrides.summary: A sourced 1650-1920 regional history separating states and colonies, with daily life, labor, Jawi writing, medicine, toilets and map warnings.

batchIdentityNotes: Targeted only exact id malaya: name Malaya, approximately 1650-1920, kind state, datesApproximate true, and missing a card before integration.

All ten target features repeat the same two-part MultiPolygon with 178 coordinate positions and bounds approximately 100.1404,0.7264 to 119.0442,6.8996. Coordinate transform noise does not create meaningful border change.

Point tests place Malacca, Johor Bahru, Kuala Lumpur, Penang and Kota Kinabalu inside, but Kota Bharu, Kuala Terengganu, Singapore, Phuket, Pattani, Kuching and Bandar Seri Begawan outside. The feature combines western peninsular and North Borneo fragments while omitting connected territories.

The geometry cannot represent one historical polity. The card explicitly separates Johor-Riau, Malay sultanates, Straits Settlements, protected and federated states, and British North Borneo company rule.

Singapore evidence is used only as explicitly labeled regional Straits context because Singapore is outside the target polygon but historically central to treaty, port, print, rail, medical and migration networks.
Separate indexed records for malacca, malaysian-islamic-states, brunei and malaysia were inspected. No appliesTo field and no additional override are proposed.

The atlas transition from malaya to malaysia at 1920 is anachronistic. It is treated as a dataset handoff, not a political founding, collapse or independence event; official later milestones are 1957 and 1963.
